h: From royal party house to wartime hospital
p: The Pavilion began as a more modest seaside villa, and it was later transformed by the architect John Nash between 1815 and 1822 into the exotic palace you see today. Queen Victoria was never a fan, and she sold it to the town of Brighton in 1850, which is why it belongs to the city now.

During the First World War, the Pavilion was used as a military hospital for Indian soldiers wounded on the Western Front. It is a moving part of its story, and the Indian Memorial Gateway at the southern entrance to the garden was given as a thank-you by the people of India.

Inside, don't miss the Great Kitchen, with its cast-iron columns shaped like palm trees, and the Music Room, with its dazzling ceiling and lotus-shaped lights. The Banqueting Room chandelier, held by a silver dragon, is one of those sights that sticks in the memory.

Allow around an hour and a half for the Pavilion. Brighton Museum and Art Gallery sits in the same garden, and Brighton Dome, built as the prince's stables, is right next door, so you can easily make a morning of it before heading down to the beach.
Tip: in peak season the Pavilion can get busy, so arriving early in the day often means a calmer look around the most popular rooms.
